title: Tag sound recordings even when their filenames are misleading
summary: People collect recordings with names such as final2.wav or tags copied from another file. A sound organiser should still recognise the recording and admit when the available clues disagree.
audience: People organising sound recordings and media libraries.
why_it_matters: Wrong descriptions can make a useful recording hard to find.
proposed_fix: Teach a small model when to trust the recording and when to trust its description, then test whether it can safely use a broader label.
example: A clip called birds.wav contains a door closing. The system should rely on the sound, or use a broad label, instead of confidently repeating the filename.
flow: Use public recordings' existing features.
Train and compare small labeling models.
Test new uploaders with clean, absent and conflicting descriptions.
deliverable: A trained small labeling model and evidence about when it should give a precise label, a broad label or no answer.
question: Can it still label recordings reliably when descriptions are missing or misleading?
measure: Correct labels, confident mistakes, useful broad labels and computer time.
baseline: Majority/top-level frequency and metadata-only text classification. Audio-only logistic regression and concatenation of the same frozen features. Simple probability averaging, fixed metadata dropout, and calibrated hierarchical fallback. Published HATR attention-fusion baseline and a conservative audio-parent-consistent metadata gate. Use a clean implementation if the official baseline code license remains unresolved; do not silently omit these strong alternatives.

The contribution is a controlled reliability/coverage/parameter-budget study under fixed representations and matched data, separating clean, missing and contradictory metadata; a negative result is valid.
proposed_difference: A controlled study of reliability and model size when sound and descriptions disagree.
risk: Artificially wrong descriptions may not resemble real mistakes; previous exposure of the pretrained encoder is not fully known.
data_plan: Public sound features and descriptions. A real feature file and all metadata were opened; 9,304 clips have CC0/CC-BY item licenses. No large audio download is required.

summary: A practice tool can tell a guitarist that a correct note is an octave too high when the microphone or pickup emphasises harmonics. A compact adapted model could make this feedback more dependable.

flow: Audit paired single-note intervals.

technical_detail.research_question: Can a small contrastive adapter on a compact code-retrieval model improve robustness to identifier/documentation shortcuts while preserving retrieval quality and CPU efficiency?
technical_detail.hypothesis: An adapter trained with identifier-masked retrieval text and hard negatives will reduce the performance drop under controlled naming changes, with a measurable trade-off on ordinary unmodified code.

model.backbone: LateOn-Code-edge, a 17M-parameter late-interaction retriever with 48-dimensional token vectors.
model.adaptation: Freeze the encoder and cache token embeddings; learn a small residual low-rank projection with contrastive/hard-negative and naming-consistency objectives. Compare against the unchanged released projection.
model.parameters: For a rank-8 residual adapter over 48-dimensional vectors, about 768 projection weights plus any biases. Fix query/document token budgets across comparisons.

Group all functions' transformed versions and exact/near duplicates; split modules/classes together. Identifier masking changes retrieval text only and is not claimed to be a semantics-preserving executable program transformation. Manually review a fixed random sample of retrieved alternatives to address multiple relevant functions.

title: Give a new user useful film recommendations from a few ratings
summary: A new user has little history, so a recommender often falls back to the same popular films. A small adaptation model can test how much personalisation is possible after only a few ratings.
audience: People studying personalisation in consumer software.
why_it_matters: With only a few ratings, a recommender may fall back to the same popular items for everyone.
proposed_fix: Adapt a compact recommender to a new user and study the trade-off between relevance, personalisation and catalogue coverage.
example: After rating three older comedies, a user should receive relevant candidates without the list being dominated entirely by the most rated blockbusters.
flow: Build strictly separated earlier-user/later-user cohorts.
Train a compact item model and a small new-user adapter.
Test support size, tied rating times, relevance and catalogue coverage.
deliverable: Conditional on a substantial study design, an adaptation model and a careful new-user/time/popularity evaluation.
question: How useful can recommendations become after one, three or five ratings?
measure: Relevant films near the top, how widely recommendations cover the catalogue, popularity concentration and computer cost.
baseline: Global popularity and genre-weighted popularity. Matrix factorisation with a fitted new-user vector. LightGCN item-embedding mean/ridge adaptation and a head without popularity correction.
alternative: October DeepCommerceRec already combines graph/sequence/context information and evaluates cold-start/temporal settings. The October 29 IGDM source was abstract-only and is corroboration, not a fully inspected method. The proposed contribution is a narrower adaptation/coverage trade-off with transparent CPU cost and stronger timestamp-tie accounting; no novelty guarantee.
proposed_difference: Potential evidence about small-history adaptation under temporal, popularity and CPU constraints.

technical_detail.research_question: Under a CPU budget and 1/3/5 initial ratings, can a compact adaptation head over pretrained item embeddings improve new-user ranking without reducing catalogue coverage or over-amplifying popularity?
technical_detail.hypothesis: A regularised history-to-user embedding head with a learned popularity correction will outperform a simple average of liked-item embeddings at small support sizes, but the ranking/coverage trade-off will vary with the popularity of a user's history.

model.adaptation: Freeze item embeddings and learn a small history-to-user mapping/gate plus regularised popularity correction. Encode rating values and support count; compare a simple weighted mean and per-user ridge/gradient adaptation.
model.parameters: Warm embeddings on the order of a few hundred thousand parameters; small new-user head below 50,000.

technical_detail.design: Use global timestamp cutoffs and wholly held-out new users; pretraining graph edges cannot include those users or later ratings. The feasibility probe found 874 of 1,811 users had a timestamp tie at the five-rating boundary, so item-ID tie ordering cannot silently define ground truth. Rank the entire eligible catalogue rather than 100 easy sampled negatives.
